item.title: Re: It's An Anomalous World
item.content:encoded: Hart Island. An uninhabited island near NYC that's been home to a barracks, a POW camp, a mental asylum, a sanitarium, a homeless shelter, a reformatory school, a rehab center, and a prison, now used as a mass grave for unclaimed and unidentified remains, miscarriages, and stillbirths. The burials here are carried out by inmates, and the bodies are frequently mixed up and put in the wrong plots. Past a certain point, no more records exist of who's buried where. It's borderline impossible to visit, since it's still part of the Department of Corrections, and the waters around it are treacherous and full of rocks. Nothing inherently anomalous about any of that, but the negative energy around this place must be insane.

item.title: Re: It's An Anomalous World
item.content:encoded:
A shark born without skin or teeth was recently caught by a fishing trawler off the coast of Sardinia. Though dead by the time it was discovered in the trawler's haul, has been estimated to be about 3 years old, and an otherwise healthy example of the blackmouth catshark species.

It is currently believed that its condition was simply a very weird genetic mutation, but researchers are looking into possible pollution factors as well, whether as a congenital cause or as a cause for the mutation.

The reason for the lack of teeth ties into some interesting secondary real-world weirdness: the teeth of sharks and their evolutionary siblings are essentially really big scales that use some of the standard procedural programming for chordate teeth They grow from the gums rather than the jaw- ergo, no gums, no teeth. When you see those megalodon jaws with teeth, the jaw is usually more like a really fancy display case: even in the rare cases where a preserved jaw is found with it's original teeth, there's nothing to hold them in place except some grooves.

item.title: Re: It's An Anomalous World
item.content:encoded:
Like surely something could be or is tampering with our brains, to make us believe this stuff!

I mean, kinda? It makes sense when you know how memory works. Long unasked-for ramble incoming.Take three principles:

+ show block
– hide block

1) Memory is association-based.
- The way we put things into memory is by making connections; between the current situation and facts/sensations already in memory, between things happening at the same time, etc.
2) we only remember the gist.
- Our capacity for long term memory has no limit we've found yet, but the amount of info you can transfer into long term memory at any one time is very limited. Nowhere near enough to transfer every aspect of a current situation (like recording a video). So, we only store a high-level summary of any given event or time. (We aren't 100% in conscious control of what goes into that summary.)
3) Rememembering = reconstruction.
- When you retrieve (say, pull on) that gist summary later, you don't still have the info to fill it in. Instead, you fill in the gaps using all the other associations that got "pulled on" with the gist. Unfortunately, a lot of that stuff is either irrelevant to the memory or goes against what actually happened. For example, if a lawyer asks a leading question, that question can actually change the memory because it becomes part of the web of associations and gets "pulled out" with the original summary.
Point 3.5, you aren't in control of the reconstruction. To you, the memory might seem perfectly clear and complete.

People call this a bias, but it's really incredibly efficient and has a lot of positive effects as well.

The Mandella effect just shows that everyone's memory fails in similar ways, like remembering a common spelling instead of an uncommon one, or mixing multiple memories together (there's that web again), or just being slightly racist/ignorant of world affairs. (I'm really not a fan of how that's the one the populace named it after.)

item.title: Re: It's An Anomalous World
item.content:encoded: Necropost, but we've figured out a lot of the history behind it. The oldest exact copy of the S has been found on a carpet in a painting from the year 1531. Likely, the design was used as a signature across several products sold by various products around the start of the 16th century and began to spread do its simple and easily-replicable design. Afterwards, schoolchildren began to popularize it in various countries after WWII, turning it into the widespread phenomenon we know.

item.title: Re: It's An Anomalous World
item.content:encoded:
A while back, in order to test a hypothesis of how the brain functions, codes, and stores memories, a biologist performd what he called "shufflebrain" on a bunch of salamander larvae.

And it highlights the sheer WTF? that nature sometimes throws at us.

Salamander larvae have an instinct to start hunting more-or-less after they hatch. Pretty normal as things go.

So, the doctor firat pulls out large portions of the brains in some larvae. Once the larvae recover, they… slowed down on the feeding. Ok, pretty normal, the guy DID give them brain damage, after all.

Then things went to hell.

On the next batch, he started doing weird things. Like flipping the brains 180 degrees so it was upside down in their skulls, rotated each hemisphere separately, and even made the left and right hemispheres switch places. No behavioral change in the salamander larvae.

He started shifting around the parts of the brain in the larvae, such as switching the places of the midbrain and the cerebrum. No behavioral change in the salamander larvae.

Finally, in a fit of what I like to imagine as him falling deep into the "Mad Scientist" routine, our biologist proceeded to switch brain parts between the larvae of two seperate salamander species. Still no changes to the salamander larvae's behavior.

To reiterate, The only thing that seemed to affect the salamder larvae was the lack of a brain.

… So, salamander brains are plug-n-play?

The Western Magnetic Anomaly

Apparently, the Earth's magnetic Field tends to wobble, and occasionally flip. And it may be doing so Right NOW.

the Earth's magnetic field is mostly uniform, except for an area over South America, where it is almost exactly opposite of projections. And it is GROWING. It covers about 20% of the Earth now.

As for what happens when it flips… We dont really know. Most likely, little if anything. There is no evidence that the geomagnetic reversal is correlated with any mass extinctions.

item.title: Re: It's An Anomalous World
item.content:encoded:
Just put these puppies into a posted article, but I want to geek out even more about how freaking weird the life cycle of the giant tube worm is.

Behold, a pale cluster of mysterious tubes in the crushing depths of the ocean.
And toxic chemicals followed with them.

Female tube worms release eggs into the water which float upwards; males release sperm which swim after their counterparts. Normal for aquatic creatures so far. The ones that successfully fertilize then swim back down and attach themselves to rocks near sulfurous volcanic vents on the ocean floor.

Almost as soon as they start growing, they essentially become infected with single-celled archaea, with which they have a symbiotic relationship. Archaea used to be called archaebacteria but have a different internal structure — they're named that because they may have been some of the first life to evolve, ever, back in the good old "earth is a volcanically active primordial soup" days. These single-celled lifeforms can digest things that are terrifically toxic to almost all other forms of life, such as nitrite, hydrogen sulfide and ammonia — which happen to be plentiful at the foot of volcanic vents which continually belch out superheated smoke.

The worms' bodies become completely infested with archaea, to the point where they comprise about 50% of its mass. They essentially act as a digestive system, extruding oxygen and the basic building blocks of amino acids out of the toxic water and giving it to the worms.

Giant tube worm blood is super weird as a result. Look at this stuff:

To transport nitrate to the bacteria, R. pachyptila concentrate nitrate in their blood, to a concentration 100 times more concentrated than the surrounding water. The exact mechanism of R. pachyptila’s ability to withstand and concentrate nitrate is still unknown.

…tube worm hemoglobins are remarkable for carrying oxygen in the presence of sulfide, without being inhibited by this molecule as hemoglobins in most other species are.

Riftia pachyptila has the fastest growth rate of any known marine invertebrate.

All hail our tube worm overlords.

item.title: Re: It's An Anomalous World
item.content:encoded:
The Ol Doinyo Lengai volcano near Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania often produces large amounts of dark sand during its periodic eruptions. This combined with the powerful and steady winds in the area, results in the formation of huge dunes that migrate away from the volcano.

This is not so unusual.

What is unusual, however, is that this particular volcano produces sand with an extremely high iron content, creating a collective magnetic field strong enough that if you pick up a handful and throw it in the air, it will clump together and fall back onto the dune. As a result, rather than dispersing, these dunes steadily crawl like amoebas across the savannah at about 10 meters per year, steamrolling anything in their path.

item.title: Re: It's An Anomalous World
item.content:encoded:
Chiming in to note that this has been the focus of an interesting shift in how terrorism is understood in the modern context. It's existed as a tactic for a long time, but there have been some recent changes in how it's typically thought about that are related to the advent of suicide attacks.

Late 20th century studies on suicide terrorism (usually by psychologists) tended to be focused on profiling individual actors with the goal of showing it to be a fundamentally irrational act by people who would otherwise be predisposed to, well, suicide. This leaked outside the specific act being examined, and terrorism in general was often portrayed in the way being described here.

Modern terrorism scholarship (generally, not unanimously) sees terrorism as a whole, including suicide attacks, as a tactic adopted for rational reasons that is aimed at achieving specific goals that would otherwise be unattainable. Unless you're in very specific parts of the world, it's not very likely that you're in significant danger of being attacked in this way.

One thing a lot of people don't know/get is that rocket tests have to have some sort of expendable payload like that: You're testing whether the rocket can get a heavy object from here to orbit, so if you don't have a heavy object on there, it's sort of pointless… but you also don't want to put a hugely expensive probe on a rocket that could end up in the Pacific (or even slightly missing the target orbit, like the car did, thus indicating some needed tweaks to the thrust controls).

TL,DR: Basically it was the car or a weighted companion cube boring hunk of metal, and one of those options is a hell of a lot more interesting.
